content: Crop Disease Management Guide — ICAR/KVK Reference TOMATO DISEASES 1. Early Blight (Alternaria solani) Symptoms: Small brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves, surrounded by yellow halo. Spots enlarge and merge, causing leaf drop. Spreads upward. Cause: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani, favored by warm (24-29°C) humid conditions. Chemical Control: Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L water, or Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 2g/L. Spray every 7-10 days. Organic Control: Neem oil 1500 PPM at 5ml/L, or Trichoderma viride 5g/L. Apply in evening. Prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds, practice crop rotation (avoid solanaceous crops for 2 years), maintain plant spacing, avoid overhead irrigation. 2. Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans) Symptoms: Water-soaked dark brown lesions on leaves and stems with white fungal growth on undersides. Fruits develop firm brown rot. Spreads very rapidly in cool humid weather. Cause: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Favored by cool (10-25°C) humid conditions. Chemical Control: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb 72% WP at 2.5g/L, or Cymoxanil + Mancozeb. Spray immediately at first appearance. Organic Control: Copper-based fungicide (Copper hydroxide) at 3g/L. Bordeaux mixture 1%. Prevention: Avoid late evening irrigation, remove infected plant debris, use resistant varieties (Arka Rakshak, PKM-1). 3. Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. lycopersici) Symptoms: Yellowing of lower leaves, wilting during hot part of day, eventual plant collapse. Brown discoloration of vascular tissue visible when stem is cut. Control: Soil drenching with Carbendazim 50% WP at 1g/L. Trichoderma viride 4g/kg seed treatment for prevention. Prevention: Grafting tomato on wilt-resistant rootstocks, crop rotation, soil solarization. 4. Leaf Mosaic Virus (Tobacco Mosaic Virus - TMV) Symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green patches on leaves, leaf distortion, stunted growth. Control: No direct chemical cure. Neck rot causes panicle to break and fall. Most devastating rice disease worldwide. Chemical Control: Tricyclazole 75% WP at 0.6g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC at 1.5ml/L. Apply at boot leaf stage. Organic Control: Silicon-based fertilizers increase blast resistance. Pseudomonas fluorescens 5g/L spray. Prevention: Balanced fertilization (avoid excess nitrogen), use blast-resistant varieties (MTU 7029, Jyothi, IR 64), maintain optimum plant spacing. 2. Brown Spot (Helminthosporium oryzae) Symptoms: Oval or circular brown spots on leaves and glumes. Spots have yellow halo. Indicates nutrient stress (particularly potassium deficiency). Control: Mancozeb 75% WP at 2g/L. Correct potassium deficiency with MOP 25 kg/ha. Prevention: Balanced fertilization, use certified seeds, treat seeds with Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% at 3g/kg. 3. Bacterial Leaf Blight (Xanthomonas oryzae) Symptoms: Water-soaked yellow stripes on leaf margins progressing to straw-yellow or white. Spreads downward. Kresek phase causes seedling death. Control: No effective curative fungicide. Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP at 3g/L. Avoid excess nitrogen. Prevention: Use resistant varieties, treat seeds with bleaching powder 25g/10L, avoid transplanting from infected nurseries. WHEAT DISEASES 1. Fusarium/Verticillium Wilt Symptoms: Yellowing and browning of leaves starting from margins, wilting, death of plants. Brown vascular discoloration. Control: Seed treatment with Carbendazim 2g/kg. Soil drench with Carbendazim + Thiram. Prevention: Crop rotation with non-host crops, use wilt-resistant Bt cotton hybrids. 2. Leaf Curl Virus (Cotton Leaf Curl Disease - CLCuD) Symptoms: Upward or downward curling of leaves, thickening of veins, development of leaf-like structures (enations) on underside. Control: Control whitefly vector with Imidacloprid 17.8 SL at 0.5 ml/L or Thiamethoxam 25 WG at 0.3g/L. Prevention: Use CLCuD-tolerant varieties, destroy infected plants, remove weed hosts. GENERAL IPM (INTEGRATED PEST MANAGEMENT) PRINCIPLES 1. Monitor fields regularly (twice a week) 2. Record pest populations and keep spray diary 3. Use Economic Threshold Levels (ETL) to decide when to spray 4. Prefer biological control agents (Trichoderma, Pseudomonas, Beauveria bassiana) 5. Use resistant varieties as first defense 6. Alternate fungicide/insecticide groups to prevent resistance 7. Read and follow label instructions carefully 8. Wear protective equipment when spraying 9. Do not spray within 7 days of harvest (pre-harvest interval)

title: Fertilizer Nutrition Guide
content: Fertilizer and Plant Nutrition Guide for Indian Farmers UNDERSTANDING NPK Nitrogen (N): Essential for vegetative growth, leaf development, and green color. Deficiency causes yellowing of older leaves first. Sources: Urea (46% N), Ammonium Sulphate (21% N), DAP (18% N). Phosphorus (P): Essential for root development, flowering, and fruit set. Deficiency causes purple/red coloration of leaves and poor root growth. Sources: DAP (46% P2O5), Single Superphosphate - SSP (16% P2O5), Triple Superphosphate - TSP (46% P2O5). Potassium (K): Essential for disease resistance, fruit quality, and water regulation. Deficiency causes brown leaf margins. Sources: MOP/Muriate of Potash (60% K2O), SOP/Sulphate of Potash (50% K2O). MICRONUTRIENTS Zinc (Zn): Deficiency causes khaira disease in rice — white/brown spots on new leaves. Apply Zinc Sulphate 25 kg/ha as basal dose. Boron (B): Critical for fruit set, pollen germination. Deficiency in cauliflower causes hollow stem. Apply Borax 10 kg/ha. Iron (Fe): Deficiency causes yellowing between leaf veins (interveinal chlorosis) starting from young leaves. Apply Ferrous Sulphate 25 kg/ha or foliar spray. Sulphur (S): Promotes protein synthesis and oil content (important for oilseeds and onion). Apply Gypsum/SSP. Premium rates are very low: 2% for Kharif crops, 1.5% for Rabi crops, and 5% for annual commercial and horticultural crops. The government pays the remaining premium. Farmers can enroll through Common Service Centres, banks, or the PMFBY portal (pmfby.gov.in). The scheme covers all food crops, oilseeds, and annual commercial crops. content: ICAR Tomato Production Guide — Global Reference INTRODUCTION Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is one of the most important vegetable crops globally. It is grown extensively across South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America in both Kharif/wet (June-September) and Rabi/dry (October-February) seasons. SOIL AND CLIMATE Tomato grows well in well-drained red sandy loam or black loam soils with pH 6.0–7.0. The crop requires a temperature range of 20–32°C. Excessive humidity above 85% promotes fungal diseases. Rainfall of 600–1200 mm annually is suitable. VARIETIES Recommended varieties for tropical/subtropical conditions: - Arka Vikas: High yielding, suitable for Kharif/wet season - Arka Rakshak: Disease resistant, hybrid, recommended for small farmers - COTH-3: Tolerant to early blight and bacterial wilt - PKM-1: Good for fresh market, medium duration - Pusa Ruby, Roma (suitable for processing) - Local hybrids adapted to specific agro-climatic conditions LAND PREPARATION Deep plough the field 2-3 times. Apply 25 tonnes of well-rotted farmyard manure (FYM) per hectare before transplanting. Form raised beds or ridges for better drainage. NURSERY AND TRANSPLANTING Sow seeds in nursery beds at 600g per hectare. Transplant 25-30 day old seedlings at 60cm x 45cm spacing (main season) or 45cm x 30cm (short season). Transplant in the evening to reduce transplanting shock. FERTILIZER MANAGEMENT Apply NPK at 120:60:60 kg per hectare as basal dose. Top dress with 40 kg N per hectare at 30 days after transplanting and again at 45 days. Micronutrient spray of 0.5% zinc sulfate at 15 and 30 days after transplanting improves fruit quality. IRRIGATION Irrigate immediately after transplanting. Subsequently irrigate every 4-5 days in summer and 7-10 days in winter. Drip irrigation saves 40% water compared to flood irrigation and reduces foliar disease incidence. Critical irrigation stages: transplanting, flowering, fruit development, and fruit ripening. content: IRRIGATION Irrigate immediately after transplanting. Subsequently irrigate every 4-5 days in summer and 7-10 days in winter. Drip irrigation saves 40% water compared to flood irrigation and reduces foliar disease incidence. Critical irrigation stages: transplanting, flowering, fruit development, and fruit ripening. DISEASE MANAGEMENT Early Blight (Alternaria solani): Symptoms: Circular brown spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves. Management: - Spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 2g/L water at 10-day intervals - Remove and destroy infected leaves - Avoid overhead irrigation - Use resistant varieties like COTH-3 Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans): Symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves turning brown-black with white fungal growth. Management: - Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold) at 2.5g/L - Improve air circulation by proper spacing - Avoid excessive nitrogen application Fusarium Wilt: Symptoms: Yellowing of lower leaves, wilting despite adequate soil moisture, brown discoloration of vascular tissue. Management: - Use wilt-resistant varieties - Soil treatment with Carbendazim 1g/L before transplanting - Crop rotation with non-host crops for 3 years Tomato Leaf Curl Virus: Transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Use Imidacloprid 70% WG at 5g per 15L water to control whitefly. Use virus-free seedlings. PEST MANAGEMENT Fruit borer (Helicoverpa armigera): Major pest. Use pheromone traps (5/ha) for monitoring. Spray Spinosad 45% SC at 2.5ml per 10L water or Emamectin benzoate 5% SG at 0.5g/L. HARVESTING Fruits are ready 60-80 days after transplanting depending on variety. Harvest when fruits turn light pink to red. Average yield: 25-30 tonnes per hectare for hybrid varieties, 15-20 tonnes for open-pollinated varieties. MARKET Peak production months vary by climate zone: January-March and July-September in tropical areas. Sell through local APMC / mandi, online platforms (eNAM in India), or cooperative markets. Price range: Rs 500-3000/quintal in India; equivalent local market rates in other countries. Check Agmarknet (agmarknet.gov.in) for real-time mandi prices across India.

title: Irrigation Methods
content: IRRIGATION METHODS FOR INDIAN AGRICULTURE — ICAR-NWPCA INTRODUCTION India uses 80% of its freshwater for agriculture. Efficient irrigation is critical for sustainable food production. Choosing the right irrigation method depends on crop type, soil texture, water availability, topography, and farm economics. Modern precision irrigation can save 30–70% water compared to traditional flood irrigation while maintaining or improving yields. FLOOD (FURROW / SURFACE) IRRIGATION Description: Water applied across the entire field surface or in furrows between crop rows. Most common and traditional method. Suitable for closely-spaced crops (rice, wheat) and fields with uniform slope. When to use: Puddled paddy fields, fine-textured heavy clay soils with low permeability, fields with good levelling, where water is abundant and cheap. Water efficiency: 40–60% (40–60% of applied water actually reaches the crop root zone). Limitations: High water wastage through deep percolation and run-off. Promotes weed growth. Unsuitable for sandy soils. Increases risk of waterlogging and soil compaction. Requires well-levelled fields. DRIP IRRIGATION Description: Water delivered directly to the root zone through a network of pipes, tubes, and emitters at very low flow rates. Highly targeted application — virtually no wastage. When to use: Orchards, vineyards, vegetables (tomato, cucumber, capsicum, brinjal), sugarcane, cotton, banana, pomegranate, guava. Ideal for undulating terrain, sandy soils, water-scarce regions, high-value crops. Water efficiency: 85–95%. Benefits: - Reduces water use by 40–50% vs flood irrigation. - Fertilizers applied through drip (fertigation) improve nutrient use efficiency by 30–40%. - Reduced weed growth between rows. - No soil compaction from tractor passages. - Better fruit quality and uniformity. Setup cost: Rs 40,000–80,000/ha depending on system type. Government subsidy available under PMKSY (50–90% subsidy for small/marginal farmers). Maintenance: Flush laterals weekly. Check and clean emitters monthly. Filter inlet water. Winterise by draining pipes before frost in cold regions. SPRINKLER IRRIGATION Description: Water pumped through pipes

Types: - Portable sprinkler: aluminium pipes, most common for annual crops. - Semi-permanent: underground mains with portable laterals. - Micro-sprinkler: used in orchards, covers 2–5 m radius, excellent for young trees. - Rain-gun sprinkler: covers large area (30–50 m radius), suitable for sugarcane and open field vegetables. Scheduling: Irrigate during cooler hours (early morning or evening) to minimise evaporation losses. Avoid irrigation during high winds (>15 km/h). Each irrigation should bring soil to field capacity. DEFICIT IRRIGATION STRATEGY Concept: Deliberately apply less water than full crop demand during less sensitive growth stages to save water with minimal yield loss. For wheat: Maintain full irrigation at crown root initiation, tillering, jointing, and grain filling. Can skip one irrigation at boot stage with <5% yield loss. For cotton: Full irrigation at squaring to boll development. Allow mild stress at seedling and late boll opening stages. For rice: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) — let soil dry 15 cm below surface before re-irrigation. Saves 25–30% water with no yield reduction. title: Organic Farming Guide
content: ORGANIC FARMING GUIDE — NCOF (NATIONAL CENTRE OF ORGANIC FARMING) INTRODUCTION Organic farming is a production system that maintains and improves the health of soils, ecosystems, and people through use of natural inputs and elimination of synthetic chemicals. In India, organic farming is growing rapidly — over 3.9 million ha under certified organic cultivation. Key markets: domestic health food, export (Europe, USA, Japan). COMPOSTING Composting converts farm waste (crop residues, animal dung, kitchen waste) into a stable, nutrient-rich soil amendment. Good compost provides all macro and micronutrients plus beneficial microorganisms. Pit composting method: Dig a pit 2–3 m × 1.5 m × 1 m deep. Alternate 15 cm layers of green material (crop residue, leaves) and 5 cm layers of fresh dung. Sprinkle with water to maintain moisture at 50–60%. Turn the pile every 30 days for aeration. Compost is ready in 90–120 days when dark brown, crumbly, and earthy-smelling. Application rate: 10–15 t/ha for general crops; 20–25 t/ha for vegetables. Incorporate into soil 2–4 weeks before planting. Vermicomposting: Use Red Earthworms (Eisenia fetida). Layer 15 cm bedding material, add kitchen/crop waste, maintain 60–70% moisture. Harvest after 45–60 days when worm casts dominate the bed. Apply 2–3 t/ha. Provides higher nitrogen and phosphorus than ordinary compost. GREEN MANURE CROPS Green manures fix atmospheric nitrogen and add organic matter when ploughed under. Sow before the main crop or as intercrops. Recommended species: - Dhaincha (Sesbania bispinosa): fastest growing, fixes 100–150 kg N/ha in 45–60 days. Ideal for rice-based systems. - Sunnhemp (Crotalaria juncea): deep-rooted, drought-tolerant, fixes 80–100 kg N/ha. - Cowpea: dual-purpose (grain + green manure), fixes 60–80 kg N/ha. - Berseem (Egyptian clover): winter green manure, fixes 50–70 kg N/ha. - Cluster bean (Guar): drought-tolerant, suitable for dryland areas. Plough under at 50% flowering stage when biomass and nitrogen content

title: Pest Management Guide
content: INTEGRATED PEST MANAGEMENT (IPM) GUIDE — NCIPM, NEW DELHI INTRODUCTION Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is a science-based approach that combines multiple pest management strategies to keep pest populations below economically damaging levels while minimising risks to human health, the environment, and non-target organisms. IPM does not eliminate all pests — it manages them to acceptable levels. IPM PRINCIPLES 1. Prevention: Use resistant varieties, crop rotation, sanitation, and proper plant spacing to prevent pest build-up. 2. Monitoring: Regular scouting (field visits) to identify pest species, counts, and natural enemies. Do not spray based on calendar — spray based on pest population thresholds. 3. Decision: Compare observed pest populations with Economic Threshold Levels (ETLs). Spray only when ETL is crossed. 4. Intervention: Use biological controls first; cultural controls second; chemical controls as last resort and with least harmful products. COMMON PESTS AND MANAGEMENT BY CROP RICE PESTS Stem borer (Scirpophaga incertulas): Causes 'dead heart' in vegetative stage and 'white ear' at maturity. ETL: 5% dead hearts at vegetative, 1 white ear/m² at reproductive stage. Management: Clip and destroy infested nursery shoots. Remove 'dead hearts'. Pheromone traps (5/ha). Biological: Trichogramma japonica (egg parasitoid) @ 1 lakh/ha at egg mass stage. Chemical (if ETL crossed): Chlorpyrifos 20% EC @ 2.5 mL/L or Fipronil 0.3% GR @ 20 kg/ha. Brown Planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens): Feeds on phloem sap, causes 'hopper burn' (circular patches of dried plants). ETL: 10–15 hoppers per hill. Management: Grow resistant varieties (IR 64, MTU 1010). Drain field intermittently. Avoid excessive nitrogen. Preserve natural enemies (spiders). Chemical: Buprofezin 25% SC @ 1 mL/L or Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.25 mL/L. Never use pyrethroids — they cause BPH resurgence. title: Post Harvest Guide
content: POST HARVEST MANAGEMENT GUIDE — ICAR-CIPHET LUDHIANA INTRODUCTION India loses 15–18% of food grains and 25–40% of fruits and vegetables annually due to poor post-harvest handling. Proper storage, grading, and packaging can recover Rs 90,000 crore worth of food per year. Post-harvest management begins at the field — correct timing of harvest is as important as storage conditions. HARVESTING AT CORRECT MATURITY Cereals: Harvest wheat and rice at 18–22% grain moisture. Avoid harvesting at high moisture (>25%) as it promotes mould. Delayed harvest causes shattering losses. Combine harvesters reduce field losses to 1–2% vs 3–5% for manual harvest. Vegetables: Harvest in the morning after dew has dried. Most vegetables should be harvested at physiological maturity, not over-ripe. Tomatoes for local market: pink-red stage. For distant markets: green-turning stage. Leafy vegetables: before bolting. Onions: 50% tops down. Fruits: Mangoes: harvest when specific gravity reaches 1.01–1.02 (float test). Bananas: harvest at 75% filling. Citrus: full colour development. Grapes: 20–24° Brix (sugar content). FIELD COOLING AND HANDLING Temperature management after harvest is critical. Every 10°C reduction in temperature roughly doubles shelf life. Shade harvested produce immediately. Avoid harvesting during peak heat (10 AM–4 PM) for perishables. Hydrocooling (cold water): Effective for leafy vegetables and cucumbers. Precooling reduces field heat rapidly. Forced air cooling: Standard for grapes, strawberries, stone fruits. Achieves 90% cooling in 2–4 hours. GRADING AND SORTING Remove diseased, damaged, and undersized produce. Grading improves market value by 15–30%. Hand-grading: sufficient for small quantities. Mechanical graders: available for tomato, potato, onion, mango through horticultural co-operatives. title: Rice Cultivation Guide
content: RICE CULTIVATION GUIDE — ICAR-NRRI CUTTACK INTRODUCTION Rice (Oryza sativa) is the staple food crop of India. It is grown in three seasons: Kharif (June–November), Rabi (November–April), and Zaid (March–June). India produces approximately 120 million tonnes annually. Transplanted paddy is the dominant cultivation method in most rice-growing states. LAND PREPARATION Thoroughly puddle the field 2–3 times after flooding to achieve a mud consistency that suppresses weed germination. Final levelling with a laser leveller saves 25–30% irrigation water. For direct-seeded rice, prepare a firm, well-drained seedbed. Incorporate green manure (Sesbania) or crop residue at last tillage. SEED SELECTION AND NURSERY MANAGEMENT Choose certified seeds of recommended varieties. Soak seeds in water for 24 hours, then incubate wrapped in moist gunny for 24–48 hours until germination. Treat seeds with Carbendazim 2g/kg or Pseudomonas fluorescens 10g/kg to prevent seedling diseases. Nursery rate: 20–25 kg seed/ha for transplanted rice; 80–100 kg/ha for direct seeding. Raise nursery in well-prepared raised beds (10 cm height, 1.2 m width). Apply Cartap hydrochloride 4G @ 20 kg/ha in nursery at 10 days after sowing (DAS) to control leaf folder and stem borer. Nursery should be 21–25 days old before transplanting. TRANSPLANTING Transplant 2–3 seedlings per hill at 15 × 15 cm spacing for short-duration varieties, 20 × 15 cm for medium-duration varieties. Avoid deep planting — shallow planting at 2–3 cm depth promotes early tillering. Transplant in the afternoon to reduce transplanting stress. WATER MANAGEMENT Maintain 2–5 cm standing water from transplanting through tillering. Drain field 5–7 days before panicle initiation to suppress unproductive tillers (mid-season drainage). Maintain 2–3 cm water during panicle initiation to flowering (most critical stage). Drain 15 days before harvest to allow field to dry. Urea super granules (USG) placed 5 cm deep at transplanting improve nitrogen use efficiency by 30–40% compared to broadcast urea. WEED MANAGEMENT Critical weed competition period is 0–45 days after transplanting. Apply pre-emergence herbicide (Butachlor 50% EC at 2.5 kg a.i./ha) at 3–5 DAT in 2–3 cm standing water. Follow with one manual weeding at 30–35 DAT. Cono-weeder between rows at 20 and 40 DAT reduces weed pressure in direct-seeded rice. Use combine harvester or power reaper. Thresh within 24 hours of cutting to minimise field losses. title: Rice Disease Management
content: Rice Disease Management Guide — ICAR RICE BLAST (Pyricularia oryzae / Magnaporthe oryzae) The most devastating rice disease worldwide. Can cause 10-100% yield loss. Symptoms: - Leaf blast: Diamond-shaped lesions with grey center and brown margins - Neck blast: Infected panicle neck turns brown, causing panicle to fall (broken neck) - Node blast: Blackening of nodes, plant breaks at infected node Favourable conditions: - Temperature: 24–28°C - High humidity (>90%) - Excessive nitrogen fertilization - Night temperature below 20°C combined with high humidity Management: Chemical control: - Tricyclazole 75% WP: 0.6g per liter water — spray at first sign - Propiconazole 25% EC: 1ml per liter water - Carbendazim 50% WP: 1g per liter water - Preventive spray interval: every 10-12 days during susceptible stage Cultural control: - Use resistant varieties: Jyothi, IR-64, BPT-5204 - Balanced nitrogen application — split into 3 doses - Avoid late evening irrigation that keeps foliage wet overnight - Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest BROWN SPOT (Helminthosporium oryzae) Symptoms: Oval to circular brown spots on leaves, 1-2mm diameter with yellow halo Management: - Spray Mancozeb 75% WP (2g/L) or Hexaconazole 5% EC (1ml/L) - Treat seeds with Carbendazim 2g/kg before sowing BACTERIAL LEAF BLIGHT (Xanthomonas oryzae) Symptoms: Water-soaked leaf margins turning yellow then white. Kresek phase: Seedling wilting and death. Management: - No effective chemical control for bacterial diseases - Use resistant varieties - Avoid high nitrogen doses - Drain fields when disease appears SHEATH BLIGHT (Rhizoctonia solani) Symptoms: Oval lesions on leaf sheath at waterline, spreading upwards Management: - Validamycin 3% L: 2ml/L water - Hexaconazole 5% SC: 2ml/L water - Avoid excessive N fertilizer - Reduce plant density STEM BORER (Chilo suppressalis, Scirpophaga incertulas) Symptoms: Dead heart in vegetative stage, white ear in reproductive stage Management: - Pheromone traps: 5/ha

title: Soil Health Guide
content: SOIL HEALTH MANAGEMENT GUIDE — ICAR-NBSS&LUP INTRODUCTION Healthy soil is the foundation of productive agriculture. Soil health refers to the continued capacity of soil to function as a living ecosystem that sustains plants, animals, and humans. India has 20 major soil types, each with distinct nutritional and physical properties. Soil testing every 3 years is essential for informed fertilizer decisions. NPK ROLES AND DEFICIENCY SYMPTOMS Nitrogen (N): Essential for chlorophyll and protein synthesis. Deficiency causes yellowing (chlorosis) of older leaves first, starting from leaf tips. Crops appear pale yellow-green. Excess nitrogen causes lodging, lush growth susceptible to pests, and delayed maturity. Sources: Urea (46% N), DAP (18% N), ammonium sulphate (21% N). Phosphorus (P): Critical for root development, flowering, and seed formation. Deficiency causes purplish-red discolouration of leaves (anthocyanin accumulation), especially on undersides. Stunted root system. Phosphorus is least mobile — apply close to the root zone. Sources: DAP (46% P2O5), SSP (16% P2O5), rock phosphate. Potassium (K): Regulates water use, strengthens cell walls, improves grain quality, and resistance to lodging and diseases. Deficiency causes scorching (marginal burning) of older leaf edges. Grain filling is poor. Sources: MOP/KCl (60% K2O), SOP (50% K2O — preferred for chloride-sensitive crops). SECONDARY AND MICRONUTRIENTS Sulphur (S): Deficiency causes yellowing of young leaves (contrast with N deficiency which affects old leaves). Common in light-textured soils. Apply gypsum (CaSO4) at 250–400 kg/ha or use sulphur-containing fertilizers (SSP, ammonium sulphate). Zinc (Zn): Most common micronutrient deficiency in India, especially in rice-wheat systems. Symptoms: brown rusty spots on leaves, stunted plants. Apply ZnSO4 at 25 kg/ha as basal every 3 years. Foliar spray: ZnSO4 0.5% + lime 0.25%. Boron (B): Critical for pollen viability and fruit set. Deficiency causes hollow heart in sunflower, poor pod filling in groundnut, top die-back in cauliflower. Apply borax at 10–15 kg/ha.

content: Weather, Climate and Farming Advisory Guide MONSOON FARMING CALENDAR FOR KARNATAKA Southwest Monsoon (Kharif Season) Onset: Karnataka coast by June 1-5, interior by June 10-15. Withdrawal: October. Kharif sowing window: June 1 - July 15 for most crops. Expected rainfall zones: - Coastal/Malnad: 3000-5000mm (Dakshina Kannada, Kodagu, Shivamogga) - Northern Karnataka: 500-750mm (Bijapur, Gulbarga) - Hassan District: 1000-1300mm Northeast Monsoon / Rabi Season (October-February) Rabi sowing: October-November. Provides 10-25% of annual rainfall in interior Karnataka. Important for rabi crops, potato, onion, wheat in northern Karnataka. WEATHER IMPACT ON CROP DECISIONS High Rainfall (>150mm in 3 days): - Stop irrigation immediately - Apply drainage channels in field - Risk of root rot, Pythium damping off in vegetables - Risk of blast in rice during tillering - Avoid pesticide spray (wash-off effect) - Re-apply fungicides 48 hours after heavy rain Dry Spell (No rain for 15+ days during Kharif): - Irrigate using available water sources - Apply anti-transpirants (Kaolin 6% spray) to reduce water stress - Mulching with dry crop residues reduces soil moisture loss by 40% - Skip fertilizer application until rain/irrigation available - Focus on critical stages: flowering and grain filling need moisture most Temperature Extremes: Cold wave (<10°C): Risk to tomato, chilli, banana. Cover with agro-nets. Delay irrigation to morning. Heat wave (>42°C): Risk of flower drop in cotton, tomato. Spray 1% KNO3 (potassium nitrate) or 0.5% MgSO4 to reduce heat stress. content: WHEAT DISEASE MANAGEMENT GUIDE — ICAR-IIWBR INTRODUCTION Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is India's second most important cereal crop after rice. Diseases cause yield losses of 10–70% depending on severity and crop growth stage. Early identification and timely management are critical for protecting yield. LEAF RUST (Brown Rust) — Puccinia triticina Symptoms: Small, circular to oval, orange-brown powdery pustules on upper leaf surface. Pustules are scattered randomly and surrounded by yellow halo. Severely infected leaves turn yellow and die prematurely. The disease is most damaging when it occurs before heading. Cause: Obligate fungal pathogen Puccinia triticina. Spreads through airborne urediniospores. Favoured by moderate temperatures (15–22°C) and high humidity or leaf wetness for 6–8 hours. Management: 1. Resistant varieties: HD 2967, GW 322, K 307 show moderate to high resistance. 2. Seed treatment: Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% DS at 2.5 g/kg seed. 3. Foliar spray: Propiconazole 25% EC at 0.1% (1 mL/L water) at flag leaf stage. Repeat after 15 days if disease persists. 4. Cultural: Avoid late sowing; early-sown crops escape peak infection period. POWDERY MILDEW — Blumeria graminis f.sp. tritici Symptoms: White powdery growth (mycelium and conidia) on upper leaf surface, later turning grey-brown. Severely infected leaves turn yellow. The disease is most common in cool (15–20°C), humid, cloudy conditions. More prevalent in irrigated areas. Cause: Obligate biotrophic fungus. Unlike rusts, does not require free water — high humidity (>70%) is sufficient. Management: 1. Resistant varieties: NW 1014, HI 8498. 2.
